objectives: Place the story in time and place (about 4,000 years ago, Babylon in Mesopotamia) and name what the people worshipped.
Separate what the people did in the house of worship from what the chapter shows the statues could and could not do.

Discover that “could” changes its meaning with the context (a power people believed in / a real inability), expand short noun phrases (named …, made from …) into relative clauses and use ago / when / From to frame time.
Reach a conclusion from evidence and express it respectfully, without mocking people.
content.pedagogy: Start with an evidence test, not a lecture. Learners build a two-column chart (what the people did / what the statues could do according to the chapter) and support every line with a quoted phrase. Grammar is discovered from the key sentence: You ask “Who believes the statue can help or harm? Does the chapter show it doing that?” and learners find that the same word “could” can report a belief or state a real inability before you name the rule.
priorKnowledge: Past simple; can/could for ability; who/which for describing people and things.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners may read “a god which could help or harm him” as the narrator’s fact. It reports what people believed; the chapter shows the opposite (“They could not even move …”).
Do not reduce the chapter to laughing at the people; the point is what the evidence shows.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: “could” in context (a power people believed in · a real inability · being unable to accept an idea) · short noun phrase ↔ relative clause (a boy named Abraham = a boy who was named Abraham · statues made from wood and stone = statues which were made …) · time framing (about 4,000 years ago · when he was at a very young age · From childhood).
Notice (Activity 1): Board “He could not understand how an intelligent person could make a statue and then see it as a god which could help or harm him.” Ask only: “Who believes the statue can help or harm? Does the chapter show it doing this?” Then point to “They could not even move from one place to another on their own.” Pairs say in their own words how the two uses of “could” differ before you confirm.
Build (Activities 2–3): expand “named …” and “made from …” into full who/which clauses, then complete the time lines with ago / when / From and explain why “Since” does not fit with “was”.
Likely errors: *statues which made from wood (missing “were”) · *4,000 years before (for counting back from now) · *Since childhood, his heart was full … · reading “could” as a polite request.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about a person noticing something surprising in a new place, with one time frame, one “named / made from” phrase and one “could not understand how …”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the long opening frame and keep the name for the end: “a VEry LONG time aGO, | aBOUT four THOUsand YEARS aGO, | in the KINGdom of BAbylon | in MesopoTAmia, | there was a BOY named Abraham.”
Weak and strong forms: “could” is weak /kəd/ in “how an intelligent person could make a statue”; the negative is stressed: “They COULDn’t even MOVE”.
-ed endings: worshipped /t/, talked /t/, asked /t/, discovered /d/, named /d/, surprised /d/.
Word focus: in-TEL-li-gent, BAB-y-lon, mes-o-po-TA-mi-a, sur-PRISED, HOME-land, BEG-ging.
beforeReading: Show the Babylon hotspot image and ask: “What would you need to see before you believed that an object can hear you or help you?” Collect two or three kinds of evidence on the board (it answers, it moves, it acts) and keep them for the chart.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: Where and when does the story start?
Box the three time phrases (about 4,000 years ago / when he was at a very young age / From childhood).
Two columns: What the people did (bowed, cried, begged, asked for help, made a wish) / what the statues could do according to the chapter.
Underline the sentence that says the statues could not hear or understand the prayers.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the evidence chart in view.
Language Focus: Discover the two meanings of “could” in Activity 1, then expand the short noun phrases and frame the time in Activities 2–3.
Write four connected sentences about a person noticing something surprising in a new place.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: Babylon hotspot image, pairs agree on what would count as evidence that an object can hear or help, three ideas stay on the board; 5–12 Listen with books closed (Where? When?), then read along and box the time phrases; 12–19 Pairs build the two-column chart (the people did / the statues could or could not), every line with a quoted phrase, quick whole-class check against the evidence ideas on the board; 19–23 Quick Challenge individually; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Who believes? What does the chapter show?), Activities 2–3 in pairs while you monitor “which were made”; 31–38 Use: Learners draft four sentences about someone who visits a new place and sees something surprising (a market, a museum, a new school), two volunteers read and the class names the time frame and the “could” sentence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which actions belong to the people and which abilities does the chapter deny to the statues?
In “a god which could help or harm him”, whose belief is being reported?
How can we state a conclusion from evidence without mocking people?
interactiveTips: Use the “A House Full of Idols” hotspot to locate the scene before learners fill the “what the people did” column.
Replay “They could not even move from one place to another on their own.” and ask which column it belongs to.
Keep the evidence chart visible during Activity 1 so learners can check the meaning of “could” against it.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “The people ____ in the house of worship.” / “The statues could not ____.” / “There was a ____ named ____.” and let learners copy the time phrases from the text before writing their own.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences about a surprising place using two “could” meanings (a belief and a real inability), two short noun phrases and one “when” clause.

formativeAssessment: Separates the people’s actions from what the statues could do.
Explains the two meanings of “could” in context.
Expands a short noun phrase into a correct relative clause.
expectedResponses: The people bowed, cried and asked the statues for help, but the chapter shows that the statues did not eat, drink or talk, could not move on their own and could not hear or understand the prayers.
content.transferTask: Describe something surprising you noticed in a new place, using a time frame, one short noun phrase and one sentence with “could not understand how …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners reach the conclusion from the evidence chart and find the two meanings of “could” themselves before I confirmed them?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, build a two-column chart: what the people did, and what the statues could or could not do. Every line needs a quoted phrase.
checkQuestions: What does every line need? (a quoted phrase)
What goes in the second column? (what the statues could or could not do)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check the chart against the evidence ideas from the hook. During Activities 2–3, listen for “which were made” in the expanded noun phrase. In the Use task, ask the class to name the time frame and the could sentence after each reading.

exitTicket: Write one sentence about what the people did and one about what the statues could not do. Then expand “statues made from wood and stone” into a which-clause.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter places Abraham in Babylon in Mesopotamia about 4,000 years ago. Mesopotamia is in today's Iraq, Türkiye's neighbour.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which ancient cities of Mesopotamia and Anatolia do you know (Babylon, Ur, Göbeklitepe, Çatalhöyük near Konya)? What do they tell us about early human cultures?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe old beliefs as historical facts, without words like 'stupid' or 'primitive'. Teach 'ancient', 'early' and 'believed that'.

objectives: Distinguish Abraham’s repeated childhood habits from single events (the question about the “toys”, the Mardukh incident).
Keep Azer’s explanations (“not toys, but our gods”, “deep knowledge”) as the father’s viewpoint, not the narrator’s fact.
Discover how used to, while + past continuous and One day + past simple separate habit, background and event, and correct not … but, a comparative and a reported negative instruction.
Discuss a disagreement between parent and child respectfully.
content.pedagogy: Draw a two-layer timeline on the board: The top line holds what happened again and again, the bottom line holds what happened only once. Learners place chapter phrases on the right line and justify each choice with a signal word (often, used to, sometimes / One day). The grammar is discovered from that sorting: Learners notice that the signal words and the verb forms work together before you name used to, the past continuous and the past simple.
priorKnowledge: Past simple and past continuous; comparatives with -er; imperatives.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners may think “One day” means every day or that the two “One day” sentences are the same event.
Azer’s claim that the big ears “show his deep knowledge” is his belief; the chapter labels Mardukh as the chief god in the people’s belief.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: used to + base verb for a past habit (past simple can continue the habit: rode … kicked) · while + was/were + -ing for background · One day + past simple for a single event · not … but … to reject and replace an idea · bigger than (short adjective + -er) · tell + person + not to + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six chapter parts into “again and again” / “only one time”. Ask: “How many times did this happen? Which word told you?” Learners should find often, used to, sometimes and One day themselves.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose used to / was making / saw, then fix “and our gods” → but, “more bigger” → bigger, “don’t play” → not to play. After each item ask what the sentence means with the wrong form.
Likely errors: *was used to watch / *use to watch · *while he was make · *more bigger than · *He told his son don’t play.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about a childhood routine that led to one memorable event, with “I used to …”, “while …”, “One day …” and a reported instruction or a comparison.
content.pronunciationFocus:
used to has /s/ and a weak “to”: “he OFten /ˈjuːstə/ WATCH his FAther | while he was MAKing Idols”.
Contrastive stress in Azer’s answer: “They are NOT TOYS, | but our GODS.”
Keep the reported instruction together: “He TOLD his SON | NOT to PLAY with it aGAIN.”
Comparative: “BIGger than OURS” (no “more”).
Word focus: I-dol (/ˈaɪdl/), MAR-dukh, FA-vors, KNOWL-edge (/ˈnɒlɪdʒ/), KICKED (/t/), re-PLIED (/d/).
beforeReading: Say two sentences about yourself: One habit (“When I was a child, I used to walk to school with my grandfather.”) and one single event (“One day, I found a lost cat.”). Pairs decide which is which and tell each other one example of each.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What did Abraham do with the idols?
Underline every repeated action (watched, played, rode, kicked).
Circle both “One day” sentences and mark what happens after each.
Label Azer’s words “Azer says”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the two-layer timeline.
Language Focus: Sort habit and event in Activity 1, then choose the forms and correct the errors in Activities 2–3.
Write four connected sentences about a childhood routine and one turning point.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: One habit and one single event from the teacher, pairs share their own examples; 5–12 Listen for gist (What did Abraham do with the idols?), then read along and underline repeated actions; 12–19 Two-layer timeline on the board: Pairs copy phrases to the habit line or the event line and name the signal word, then label Azer’s words as his viewpoint; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with whole-class check (Which word told you?), Activities 2–3 individually with pair checking; 31–38 Use: A four-sentence childhood memory (I used to … while … One day … My teacher told me not to …), partners underline the habit and the single event; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which actions happened again and again, and what happened only once?
How do we report Azer’s belief without presenting it as a fact?
How can a child disagree with a parent and still speak respectfully?
interactiveTips: Use Azer’s Workshop hotspot for the habit line and The Statue of Mardukh hotspot for the single event.
Replay the first paragraph and ask learners to raise a hand at every habit signal they hear.
Do not ask learners to act out riding or kicking the statues; keep the focus on the language of habit and event.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “When I was a child, I used to ____.” / “One day, ____.” / “My ____ told me not to ____.” and a word bank of signal words (often, sometimes, One day).
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-sentence memory with two habits, one while-background, one single event, one comparison and one reported instruction.

formativeAssessment: Sorts habit and event correctly and names the signal word.
Uses used to, while + past continuous and One day + past simple accurately.
Reports a negative instruction with not to + verb.
expectedResponses: Abraham used to watch his father making idols and used to play with them; one day his father saw him riding the statue of Mardukh, got angry and told him not to play with it again.
content.transferTask: Write four connected sentences about a childhood routine that led to one memorable moment, including a reported instruction.
content.teacherReflection: Did the two-layer timeline help learners discover the difference between habit and single event before I named the forms?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, copy phrases onto the habit line or the event line of the timeline. Name the signal word for each. Then label Azer’s words as his viewpoint.
checkQuestions: How many lines are on the timeline? (two)
What do you write next to each phrase? (the signal word)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “used to watch” and “used to play” are on the habit line and “one day … saw” is on the event line. Listen in the Use task for while + past continuous. Ask partners to underline the habit and the single event in each other’s memory.

exitTicket: Write one “used to” sentence and one “One day” sentence about your own childhood, and report one instruction with “told me not to …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Azer explains that the statues are gods. The chapter keeps his words as his viewpoint.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do young people disagree with parents in Turkish culture, and how in an English-speaking family? Which words show respect in each (Baba, siz …; Dad, I see your point, but …)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Respect for elders looks different across cultures but exists in all of them. Learners avoid saying one culture has no respect.

objectives: Trace the same reasoning pattern in the star and moon episodes: possibility → observation → reason → conclusion.
Explain that disappearing, not brightness, is the evidence that changes Abraham’s view.
Discover what “still” shows, link ideas with Although / On the other hand / to / because and report a question and a conclusion (wondered if …, understood that …).
Connect humility with changing a view when evidence changes.
content.pedagogy: Teach reasoning as a pattern. Learners fill two rows of four boxes (star / moon: possibility, observation, reason, conclusion) with quoted phrases, then check whether the moon row follows the same logic as the star row. The grammar grows out of the reasoning: Learners notice that the question “Could this be …?” opens a possibility and “he understood that …” closes it, and that “still” explains why Abraham is sad before any rule is named.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners may think the star is rejected because it is small or not bright enough; the chapter gives the reason “because it sets and disappears”.
“Still” is not about being quiet or not moving.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: still + past continuous for a situation that has not changed (they were still showing …) · Although + clause · On the other hand to change viewpoint · to + verb for purpose (left his home to take a walk) · because + clause (not Despite / Because of + clause) · reported yes/no question (wondered if / whether it could be …) · reported conclusion (understood that it could not be …).
Notice (Activity 1): “Years passed … they were still showing love and respect to idols.” Ask: “Years passed. Had the people changed? Which word tells us? Why did it make Abraham sad?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the lines with Although / On the other hand / to / because and explain why Despite and Because of do not fit, then report “Could this be my Lord?” with if / whether and turn “he understood that it could not be his Lord” into Abraham’s own words.
Likely errors: *Despite he wondered · *Although …, but … · *wondered if could it be · *left his home for take a walk.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about someone testing two possible explanations for an everyday situation and reaching a reasoned conclusion.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Yes/no question rises, conclusion falls: “COULD this be my LORD?↗” / “he UNderSTOOD | that it COULD not be his LORD↘”.
Concession and change of viewpoint with pauses: “alTHOUGH he ALways WONdered about alLAH, | he ALso KNEW …”, “On the OTHer HAND, | …”.
Weak “to” in “to take a walk” (/tə/).
-ed endings: passed /t/, looked /t/, wondered /d/, disappeared /d/, faded /ɪd/.
Word focus: cre-A-tor, COUN-try-side, dis-ap-PEARED, WON-dered, SHIN-ing.
beforeReading: Give a neutral mystery: “The classroom lights suddenly go off. Could it be a power cut? Could someone have pressed the switch?” Ask what evidence would make learners drop their first explanation.
duringReading: Circle “still” and say what has not changed.
Number the four steps of the star episode.
Number the same steps for the moon episode.
Underline the reason Abraham gives for rejecting the star.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the two reasoning rows in view.
Language Focus: Discover “still” in Activity 1, link the ideas in Activity 2, then report a question and a conclusion in Activity 3.
Write a four-sentence reasoning chain about an everyday situation.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: The lights-off mystery, pairs name the evidence that would change their first explanation; 5–12 Listen and read, then circle “still” and ask what has not changed; 12–20 Reasoning rows: Pairs fill four boxes for the star and four for the moon with quoted phrases, then check with another pair whether both rows follow the same pattern and what the key evidence is (disappearing, not brightness); 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Had the people changed?), Activities 2–3 in pairs with a board check of “wondered if it could be”; 32–38 Use: A four-sentence reasoning chain about an everyday puzzle (a missing bag, a strange noise at night) with Although / because / wondered if / understood that, two pairs read and the class names the evidence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What repeats in the star and moon episodes?
Which observation makes Abraham change his mind each time?
Why is changing a view after new evidence a strength?
interactiveTips: Use The Cave hotspot for the setting and The Star and the Moon hotspot for the two observations.
Replay the star question and the moon conclusion one after the other and ask what changed in between.
Ask learners to point to the exact reason (“because it sets and disappears”) before accepting any answer.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a four-box frame: “He saw ____. He wondered if ____. When it ____, he said ____ because ____. He understood that ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two parallel reasoning chains about an everyday puzzle, using Although, On the other hand, a reported question and a reported conclusion.

formativeAssessment: Orders the four reasoning steps in both episodes.
Explains what “still” shows.
Reports a yes/no question with if / whether and statement word order.
expectedResponses: Abraham asks whether the star and then the moon could be his Lord; when each one disappears or fades, he rejects it and understands that it could not be his Lord.
content.transferTask: Compare two possible explanations for an everyday observation and show which piece of evidence changes your conclusion.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see a repeated reasoning pattern rather than two separate stories, and did they find what “still” means from the context?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, fill four boxes for the star and four for the moon with quoted phrases. Then check with another pair: do both rows follow the same pattern?
checkQuestions: How many boxes for each? (four)
Who do you check with? (another pair)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen for pairs who say brightness is the key evidence and ask “What made him say no?”. During the board check, listen for statement order after “wondered if”. Ask two pairs to read their everyday puzzle chain.

exitTicket: Report this question: “Could this be the right answer?” (She wondered …). Then write one sentence with “still”.

rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four step headings.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham changes his view after new evidence. Asking questions about the world is valued differently in different school cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: In your school, is it easy to ask 'Why?' in class? In some English-speaking classrooms students are expected to question the teacher. What are the good sides of each style?
interculturalFocus.perspective: There is no single right classroom culture. Learners name one habit from each they would like to keep.

objectives: Follow the sequence: The sun sets → Abraham’s conclusion → prayer for help → responsibility → the conversation with his father.
Explain why the same if-structure is a prayer for guidance in Abraham’s mouth and a threat in his father’s.
Use until for an end point, choose + person + to be, should + base verb + because, imperatives and stop + -ing.
Practise respectful communication when a family disagreement becomes tense.
content.pedagogy: Organize the lesson by speaker and purpose. Learners fill a three-column map (speaker / words / purpose) for every spoken line in the chapter. When the two if-sentences sit next to each other on the map, learners discover that the grammar is the same but the purpose is different because the purpose comes from the speaker and the situation. Abraham’s prayer is read intact and calmly; the father’s threat is read once by the teacher and never acted out.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners may think both if-sentences are threats or both are promises.
The father’s threat is not carried out in this chapter; do not add events.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: If + present, will + verb with two purposes (a need for guidance / a threat) · until for the end point of an action (stayed until sunrise) · choose + person + to be + role · should + base verb for a duty, + because for the reason · imperatives (follow me, Leave here now) · stop + -ing (Stop worshipping) vs stop to + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): Show the two if-sentences side by side. Ask: “Who is speaking? What does each speaker want?” Then: “Is the grammar the same?” Learners conclude that the speaker and the situation give the purpose.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose until / to be, then correct “should to guide” and “Stop worship”; ask what “Stop to worship” would mean.
Likely errors: *should to guide · *If you will not stop … · *Stop to worship (opposite meaning) · *chose him being.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences in a safe school scene: Someone realises a responsibility, says why with should … because …, gives one instruction and hears a conditional response (a warning about a consequence, never violence).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the prayer calmly with contrastive stress: “If alLAH DOESn’t SHOW me the RIGHT WAY, | I will BE on the WRONG PATH.”
The father’s line is read once by the teacher, clearly but without drama.
Weak forms: should /ʃəd/ in “he should guide his people”, to /tə/ in “chose him to be His Messenger”.
Imperatives start strong: “FOLlow me”, “STOP WORshipping IDols”, “LEAVE here NOW”.
Word focus: SUN-rise, cre-A-tions, REC-og-nized, MES-sen-ger, re-JECT, GUID-ance.
beforeReading: Say “If you don’t hurry, you’ll miss the bus.” twice: Once as friendly advice, once as a warning. Learners decide which is which and what changed (tone, speaker, situation).
duringReading: Mark the moment the sun sets and the conclusion that follows.
Fill the speaker / words / purpose map for every spoken line.
Underline the duty and its reason (should … because …).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the speaker map in view.
Language Focus: Compare the two if-sentences in Activity 1, then choose until / to be and correct should and stop in Activities 2–3.
Write a four-sentence school scene with a responsibility, an instruction and a conditional warning.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: The same if-sentence in two tones, learners name advice or warning; 5–12 Listen and read, then mark the sunset and the conclusion (Allah could not be one of the creations); 12–19 Speaker map in pairs: speaker / words / purpose for each spoken line (question, prayer for help, instruction, threat), whole-class check; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Who is speaking? What does he want?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain “stop worshipping” vs “stop to worship”; 31–38 Use: A four-sentence scene at school (a team captain, a class monitor, a lab partner) with should … because …, one imperative and one if-warning, partners label the purpose of each sentence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why do two sentences with the same grammar have different purposes?
What responsibility does Abraham recognize, and what reason does the chapter give?
How does Abraham address his father, and what does that show?
interactiveTips: Use The Setting Sun hotspot for the observation and The Right Way hotspot for the prayer and the responsibility.
Replay the two if-sentences one after the other before Activity 1.
Keep all transfer scenes safe: Warnings about missed buses or lost points, never threats of harm.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “I should ____ because ____.” / “____, please.” (imperative) / “If you don’t ____, I will ____.” in a neutral setting.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two mini-dialogues that use the same if-structure for two different purposes (help and warning) and explain the difference in one sentence.

formativeAssessment: Identifies speaker and purpose for both if-sentences.
Uses should + base verb with a reason.
Uses stop + -ing with the right meaning.
expectedResponses: When the sun set, Abraham understood that Allah could not be one of the creations; he asked Allah for guidance, recognized that he should guide his people, and his father answered his invitation with anger and a threat.
content.transferTask: Write a safe school scene with one responsibility and its reason, one instruction and one conditional warning.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners find the purpose of each if-sentence from the speaker and the situation, and did the transfer stay respectful?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, make a speaker map: for each spoken line, write the speaker, the words and the purpose. Purposes are question, prayer for help, instruction or threat.
checkQuestions: What three things do you write for each line? (speaker, words, purpose)
How many purposes can you choose from? (four)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the father’s if-sentence is labelled a threat. In Activity 1, listen for who speaks and what he wants. In the school scene, ask partners to label the purpose of each sentence.

exitTicket: Write one “should … because …” sentence about your class and one if-sentence that gives a friendly warning.

rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three events on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the speaker and purpose of both if-sentences.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read both sentences in two tones, advice and warning.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham uses the same if-structure as a prayer, and his father uses it as a threat. The same grammar can carry very different social meanings.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How does Abraham speak to his father? Which forms of address show respect in Turkish (Babacığım, siz) and in English (Dear father, please)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: English has no 'siz' form, so politeness comes from words such as please, could and would. Learners rewrite a direct instruction politely.

objectives: Compare the reason the people give (their fathers’ practice) with the evidence Abraham gives (what Allah does for him and what the statues cannot do).
Track Abraham’s effort and the people’s response: Furious, did not give up, ignored.
Use because + clause vs because of + noun, when + clause, want + person + to + verb and the meaning of “though” at the end of a sentence.
Connect patience with continuing to speak respectfully after rejection.
content.pedagogy: Organize the chapter into two kinds of reason. Learners sort quoted lines into “a reason from tradition” and “a reason from evidence” and discuss the difference without judging people. The language follows the meaning: After matching the effort and response words, learners notice that “because” and “because of this” both give reasons but need different continuations, and that “though” at the end quietly signals a result Abraham did not hope for.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “We saw our fathers worship them” is the people’s reason, not evidence that the statues have power.
Learners may think “though” at the end starts a new idea; it contrasts with Abraham’s hope that they would reconsider.
content.grammarFocus:

objectives: Reconstruct the plan, the opportunity (the celebration outside town), the actions and the final state in order.
Explain that the event is planned, not an accident, and that the largest statue is not broken on purpose.
Discover “was going to” as a future seen from the past, and use usually / so / until, did not + verb (He did not break …) and and then.
Analyse intention and consequence using evidence from the text.
content.pedagogy: Use a four-part organiser on the board: plan → opportunity → actions → final state. Learners fill each part with quoted phrases, then order the action verbs. The first Language Focus task comes from the planning sentence: You ask “When he made the plan, had he broken the idols yet?” and learners work out that “was going to” looks forward from a past moment. Keep the lesson on language and intention; nothing is broken or acted out in class.
priorKnowledge: going to for plans; decided to; so and because.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners may read “what he was going to do” as something happening at that moment.
The largest statue did not act; Abraham did not break it and hung the axe around its neck (this matters in Chapter 7).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: was going to + verb (the future seen from a past moment) with decided to / made a plan to · usually for what normally happened · so for a result (not because) · until + clause for the end of waiting · began to …, one after another, until … for start, repetition and end · did not + verb for what he chose not to do (He did not break the largest statue) · and then for the order of two actions.
Notice (Activity 1): “He made a plan to destroy all their idols, but he did not tell anyone what he was going to do.” Ask: “When he made the plan, had it happened yet? Which words show it was planned?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the lines with usually / so / until and say why because and by do not fit, then rebuild the final sentence and ask which action came first.
Likely errors: *what he is going to do · *what was he going to do (question order) · *…, because he got an axe · *He did not broke the largest statue.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about someone carrying out a careful plan in a new situation (a surprise for a friend, a class exhibition), with decided to, usually or so, until, did not + verb and and then.
content.pronunciationFocus:

The final-state phrase: “He LEFT the LARGest STATue in the TEMple | unTOUCHED”.
Word focus: cel-e-BRA-tion, ri-DIC-u-lous, FOOL-ish-ness, un-TOUCHED, HUR-ried (/d/).

Number the actions in the temple.

afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the organiser in view.

content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Plan or accident? three sentences on the board, learners name the planning words; 4–11 Listen and read, then underline decision and planning words; 11–18 Four-part organiser in pairs (plan / opportunity / actions / final state) with quoted phrases, then a quick class check that the largest statue is not broken and does not act; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Had it happened yet?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 on screen with learners explaining which action came first; 30–37 Use: Four-sentence plan story (She decided to … People usually …, so … She waited until … She did not … She … and then …), partners label plan, opportunity and actions; 37–40 Exit ticket.

objectives: Follow the investigation: The shock, the search for the person responsible, the questioning in the temple.
Identify the people’s own admission (“You are well aware that these idols don’t speak!”) and separate inner recognition from outward refusal.
Distinguish direct questions from question ideas inside a sentence, correct verb forms after heard / shocked / what, and use because, so … that and If … then … meant.
Connect humility with admitting a mistake when the evidence is clear.
content.pedagogy: Build the chapter as a chain: admission → recognition → refusal. Learners find the three sentences and connect them with arrows, so they see exactly where the evidence is accepted and where pride stops a change. Language discovery follows: Learners sort the questions and notice that a question inside a longer sentence has no question mark and uses statement order (ask that statue if it can speak). The shouting at the end is read once, calmly, by the teacher and never chanted.
priorKnowledge: Question word order; because / but; so + adjective.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The people do not accept Abraham’s message; they recognize the truth inside but refuse to admit it.
Abraham’s answer about the biggest statue is part of his argument; the statue did not act.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: direct questions (Did you harm …? Have you gone mad?) vs question ideas inside a sentence (find out who did this · ask that statue if it can speak) · hear + person + -ing · what + statement order (what they heard) · shocked to + base verb · because for the reason · so + adjective + that for a strong quality and its result · If …, then … meant for a feared consequence in the past.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five parts into “the speaker’s exact question” / “a question idea inside a longer sentence”. Ask: “Where is the question mark? After ‘if’, is it ‘can it speak’ or ‘it can speak’?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct to speak → speaking, what did they hear → what they heard, to seeing → to see, then choose because / that / meant and explain the chain of shame, pride and fear.
Likely errors: *ask if can it speak · *find out who did do this · *We heard a young man to speak · *so arrogant as they couldn’t.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences reporting a disagreement in a new situation (a lost ball, a class vote), with heard / found out, an embedded question and a because / so … that / if … then link.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Direct yes/no question rises: “Did you HARM our GODS in this WAY?↗”; wh-question falls: “Then WHY do you WORship things that CAN’T SPEAK …↘”.
The embedded question has no question tune: “ask that STATue if it can SPEAK↘”.
Degree and result: “they were SO ARrogant | that they COULDn’t acCEPT the TRUTH”.
-ed endings: gathered /d/, smashed /t/, remembered /d/, displeased /d/, shouted /ɪd/.
Word focus: dis-PLEASED, AR-ro-gant, FORE-fa-thers, SMASHED, a-WARE.
beforeReading: Neutral detective warm-up: “The class plant was knocked over during the break.” Learners ask direct questions (Who did it? Did you see it?); you report two of them (“Ayşe wants to know who did it.”) and ask what changed.
duringReading: Mark the people’s reaction when they see the temple.

afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the admission → recognition → refusal chain in view.
Language Focus: Sort the questions in Activity 1, correct the verb forms in Activity 2, then build the reason–result–consequence chain in Activity 3.

content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: Detective questions about the knocked-over plant, then the teacher reports two of them; 5–12 Listen and read, underline every question; 12–19 Chain in pairs: Find the admission, the recognition and the refusal, write each on a line and connect them with arrows, then share one chain with the class; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (question mark? word order after “if”?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Four sentences reporting a disagreement (We heard someone … / We tried to find out who … / They knew … but they were so … that … / If they …, then it meant …), two pairs read aloud; 38–40 Exit ticket.

objectives: Establish the chapter’s evidence for real danger (so big …, so strong …) without sensationalising it.
Separate what Abraham knew (Allah would never leave him alone) from what the chapter does not say he knew.
Discover why the passive leaves out the doer, and use so … that, However, because, would for the future seen from the past and was used to + verb for purpose.
Explain the unexpected outcome with the chapter’s own wording (cool, safe, a garden, in good condition).
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 secures meaning and the source boundary: Learners collect danger evidence, then sort teacher statements into “the chapter says this” / “the chapter does not say this”. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners sort sentences by whether the doer is named and discover that the passive keeps Abraham, not the people who acted, at the center. The throwing and the angel’s question are read calmly by the teacher; there is no re-enactment of any part of the fire scene.
priorKnowledge: Past simple passive (was/were + past participle); so and because; will/would.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say Abraham knew in advance how he would be saved; it says he trusted Allah and knew Allah would never leave him alone.
“was used to throw” describes the purpose of a machine; it is not “used to” for a past habit.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: passive was/were + past participle when the doer is not important (was collected, were tied, was thrown) vs active · so + adjective + that (not such + adjective alone) · However, for contrast with the sentence before · because for a reason · would for the future seen from the past (knew that Allah would never …, whatever happened, it would be …, came to see what would happen) · was used to + base verb for the purpose of an object.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six parts into “we are not told who did the action” / “the subject does the action”. Ask: “Who collected the firewood? Who tied his hands? Why does the chapter not say?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete so / that / However / because and say why such and Although do not fit, then choose happened / would / to and explain why “will” changes to “would” in a story told in the past.
Likely errors: *The fire was such big that … · *Although, Abraham stayed calm · *came to see what will happen · confusing “was used to throw” with “used to” (habit).
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about a new situation with pressure and an unexpected result (an exam, a match, a school performance), with so … that, However, because, knew / thought that … would and turned out to be.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Degree and result: “The FIRE was SO BIG | that PEOple COULDn’t apPROACH it.”
Pause before the turn: “HOWever, | Abraham STAYED CALM | beCAUSE he TRUSTed alLAH.”
Passive auxiliaries are weak: was /wəz/, were /wə/: “his HANDS and FEET were TIED”.
-ed endings: collected /ɪd/, commanded /ɪd/, tied /d/, traveled /d/, emerged /d/, cooled /d/, placed /t/.
Word focus: CAT-a-pult, ap-PROACH, e-MERGED, GA-bri-el, FIRE-wood. Keep a calm, even voice in the sentences about the fire.
beforeReading: Agree on a calm reading rule: We look at evidence, trust and outcome, and nobody acts out the fire scene. Then show the chapter title and ask learners to predict what “preparing” involves.
duringReading: Collect two sentences that show real danger.
Underline what Abraham knew and what he did (stayed calm).
Mark the sentences where the doer is not named.
Circle the words that describe the outcome (cool, safe, garden, good condition).
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and write a bridge note: One thing the chapter says Abraham knew and one thing it does not say.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on who does the action, degree and result, and the future seen from the past.
Write a calm four-sentence account of pressure and an unexpected result in a new situation.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Calm reading rule and prediction from the title; 5–15 Listen, then read along, with the teacher reading the paragraph about the catapult calmly; 15–24 Danger and calm in pairs: Two danger sentences, the sentence about Abraham’s calm and its reason, and the outcome words, each with a quote; 24–31 Says / does not say: The teacher reads four statements (He trusted Allah / He knew the fire would turn into a garden / People came from many towns / The fire burnt his hands), pairs decide and prove with the text; 31–36 Quick Challenge; 36–40 Bridge note; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the danger and calm evidence from the bridge notes; 4–13 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Who did it? Why is the doer not named?), then learners change two neutral classroom sentences from active to passive (The teacher collected the books → The books were collected); 13–21 Activities 2–3 in pairs, whole-class check of so … that and would; 21–25 Board contrast: “A catapult was used to throw …” (purpose) vs “I used to walk to school” (habit); 25–34 Use: A four-sentence account of pressure and an unexpected result (so … that, However, because, I thought that … would, It turned out to be …); 34–38 Peer check: Partners underline so … that and every would; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which details show that the danger was real?
What did Abraham know, according to the chapter, and what does it not say he knew?
Why does the chapter not name the people who tied and threw him?
interactiveTips: Use the “A Huge Fire” hotspot for the danger evidence and the Cool and Safe hotspot for the outcome.
In Lesson 2, begin from the bridge notes instead of rereading the whole chapter.
Keep the angel and the prophet out of any role-play; read their words from the text.

objectives: Explain that the people’s embarrassment did not change their anger and arrogance.
Trace claim → example → challenge → result in the conversation between Nimrod and Abraham.
Discover “yet” as an unexpected contrast, and use order / tell + person + to + verb vs let / make + person + base verb, was unable to and only … has the power.
Evaluate whether an example really proves a claim.
content.pedagogy: Treat the chapter as a claim test. Learners fill a four-box chart (Nimrod’s claim / his example / Abraham’s challenge / the result) and decide whether the example proves the claim. The language grows from the same chart: Learners notice that Nimrod uses “let” to show his power to allow and Abraham uses “make” to test it, and that neither verb takes “to”. The killing of the slave is stated once, factually; there is no role-play of the court.
priorKnowledge: can / can’t; tell someone to do something; however.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Letting a person live is not the same as giving life; the example does not prove Nimrod’s claim.
“yet” here means “but”, not “not yet”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: yet / however for an unexpected contrast · order + person + to + verb vs let + person + base verb and make + person/thing + base verb · was unable to = could not / was not able to · only X has the power = X is the only one who has the power.
Notice (Activity 1): “People felt embarrassed by the miracle, yet their anger and arrogance remained unchanged.” Ask: “After feeling embarrassed, what would we expect? Did it happen? Which word tells us it did not?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct ordered … bring → to bring, let … to live → live, make … to rise → rise, then say “was unable to” and “only Allah has the power” in another way.
Likely errors: *ordered his guards bring · *let the second slave to live · *make the sun to rise · reading yet as “not yet”.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about a new situation in which someone makes a claim and another person tests it fairly (a puzzle, a skill, a sports record), with can, so, however / yet, and was unable to or this made ….
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause and stress the turn: “… by the MIRacle, | YET their ANger and ARrogance reMAINED unCHANGED.”
Challenge question rises: “Can you MAKE the SUN RISE from the WEST?↗”
Exclusive stress: “ONly alLAH has the POWer to do THAT.”
No “to” after let/make: “let the SECond SLAVE LIVE” (/lɪv/), “MAKES the SUN RISE”.
Word focus: MIR-a-cle, em-BAR-rassed, OR-di-nar-y, AR-ro-gance, NIM-rod.
beforeReading: Make a playful claim: “I can remember the names of everyone in this school.” Ask: “What example would really test this claim? What example would not be enough?”
duringReading: Mark the contrast between embarrassment and anger.
Write Nimrod’s claim in one box.
Write the example he gives in the second box.
Write Abraham’s challenge and the result in the last two boxes.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the claim chart in view.
Language Focus: Discover “yet” in Activity 1, correct order / let / make in Activity 2 and say inability and exclusive power in other ways in Activity 3.
Write four sentences about a fair test of a claim in a new situation.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: The teacher’s playful memory claim, learners suggest a fair test and an unfair one; 5–12 Listen and read, mark the contrast in the first paragraph; 12–20 Claim chart in pairs (claim / example / challenge / result), then a whole-class vote with reasons: Does the example prove the claim?; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (What would we expect?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then a quick board contrast ordered … to bring / let … live / make … rise; 32–38 Use: Four sentences about a claim and a fair test (He said he could … so she … She made him … However, he was unable to …); 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What would we expect after the miracle, and what happened instead?
Does Nimrod’s example prove his claim? Why not?
Why does Abraham’s challenge test a different level of power?
interactiveTips: Use the Nimrod’s Claim hotspot for the claim and example and The Sun from the West hotspot for the challenge.
Replay the let- and make-sentences one after the other and ask learners what is missing after “let” and “make”.
State the killing of the slave once, factually; do not dramatise it or ask learners to act the scene.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “He claimed that ____. His example was ____. It did not prove the claim because ____. He was unable to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Invent two neutral claims, one tested with relevant evidence and one with irrelevant evidence, and explain the difference with yet, let / make and was unable to.

formativeAssessment: States the claim and evaluates whether the example is relevant.
Explains “yet” as an unexpected contrast.
Uses to after order and no to after let / make.
expectedResponses: Nimrod claims he can give life and death and shows it by letting one slave live, but Abraham asks him to make the sun rise from the west; Nimrod is unable to do this because only Allah has that power.
content.transferTask: Test a simple everyday claim with relevant evidence and explain whether the evidence proves it.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners judge the relevance of the evidence rather than retell the exchange, and did they discover the let / make pattern from the text?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, complete the claim chart: claim, example, challenge, result. Then vote with the class: does the example prove the claim? Give a reason.
checkQuestions: How many columns? (four)
What do we vote on? (if the example proves the claim)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen for reasons in the vote, not just yes or no. During the board contrast, check “ordered … to bring” and “let … live” without to. In the Use task, check for However before the result.

exitTicket: Complete: “My teacher let us ____. She made us ____. She told us to ____.” and write one sentence with “yet”.

rubricLevels.secure: States Nimrod’s claim precisely.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the claim sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Says whether the example is relevant to the claim.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Does letting one slave live prove he can give life?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains yet and uses to after order and no to after let and make.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three patterns on the board.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a reasoned conclusion about a fair test.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four-sentence frame.

interculturalFocus.notice: Nimrod claims power over life and death, and Abraham tests the claim. Critical thinking about powerful claims is a shared value.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which phrases do English speakers use to question a claim politely (What evidence is there? How do you know?)? Which Turkish phrases do the same (Kanıtın ne? Nereden biliyorsun?)
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners test claims, not people. They practise questioning a claim without insulting the person who made it.

objectives: Connect Abraham’s realisation with his decision and its purpose (to spread Allah’s message).

Keep the people and stages of the journey accurate: Sarah and Lot share his faith, the journey to Syria and Palestine, the marriage to Hagar, Ishmael’s birth, the command to travel, the valley near Safa and Marwa.
Discover that to + verb can give a purpose or an instruction, and use so that + could, decided to, During, Finally and was going to ↔ is going to.
Explain a change of place without reducing the mission to escape.
content.pedagogy: Draw a simple route line on the board: Babylon → Syria and Palestine → the lonely valley near Safa and Marwa. Learners place names and time words (During his journey, soon, One day, Finally) only where the text supports them. The Language Focus starts from a surprising question: “Does to + verb always answer ‘Why?’?” Learners sort four chapter parts and find that after command / tell + person it gives an instruction, not a purpose.
priorKnowledge: to + verb for purpose; therefore; time words for stories.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say that Sarah is Abraham’s wife; it says that she and Lot shared his faith.
Leaving Babylon is presented as a decision to spread Allah’s message elsewhere, not as running away.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to + verb for purpose (travel … to spread Allah’s message) vs command / tell + person + to + verb for an instruction (commanded Abraham to travel · told his wife to stay) · so that + subject + could (purpose with its own subject) · decided to + verb · During + noun vs while + clause · Finally for the end of a long process · realized that … was going to ↔ “Nobody is going to listen …” · Therefore for a result.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort four parts into “why someone acts” / “what someone is told to do”. Ask: “Does to + verb always answer ‘Why?’? What comes before ‘to’ in the instruction group?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose to leave / During / Finally, then turn “Abraham (pbuh) realized that nobody was going to listen to his message.” into Abraham’s own thought.
Likely errors: *decided leaving · *While his journey · *At first, they reached a lonely valley · *so that his child can teach (in a past story) · *told his wife stay.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a journey or change of place (moving house, a school trip, a new city), with realized that, therefore, decided to, to / so that, during, soon, one day and finally.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause after the result marker: “THEREfore, | he deCIDed to LEAVE BAbylon | and TRAVel to OTHer LANDS | to SPREAD alLAH’s MESSage.”
Keep the purpose together, with weak could /kəd/: “so that his CHILD could TEACH PEOple about alLAH”.
Names: SAR-ah, LOT, HA-gar, ISH-ma-el, SA-fa, MAR-wa, PAL-es-tine, SYR-i-a.
-ed endings: realized /d/, married /d/, reached /t/, traveled /d/, decided /ɪd/.
Word focus: CAM-el-back, TIR-ing, JOUR-ney, RE-al-ized.
beforeReading: Ask: “When a plan does not work in one place, is it always giving up to move somewhere else?” Pairs give one neutral example (a club that cannot use the hall trains in the park instead).
duringReading: Mark who shared Abraham’s faith.
Underline the realisation, the decision and the purpose.
Place the stages on the route line with a time word for each.
Mark the two instructions (commanded … to travel / told his wife to stay).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the route line in view.
Language Focus: Sort purpose and instruction in Activity 1, choose the journey forms in Activity 2 and change the reported thought in Activity 3.
Write five sentences about a purposeful journey or change of place.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Changing place without giving up, pairs share one neutral example; 4–11 Listen and read, then mark who shared his faith and the realisation → decision → purpose sentence; 11–19 Route line: Pairs copy the three places into their notebooks and add a time word and one quoted action at each stage, one pair completes it on the board; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Does to + verb always answer “Why?”), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Five sentences about a journey or move (I realized that … Therefore, I decided to … so that … During … Finally, …), partners circle the purpose and the time words; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Abraham realize, and what did he decide as a result?
What was the purpose of his journey?
Which words keep the stages of a long journey clear?
interactiveTips: Use the Toward New Lands hotspot for the decision and the Lonely Valley hotspot for the end of the journey.
Replay the realisation and decision sentences before the route line work.
Place names on the route line only where the chapter mentions them; do not add stops or dates.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “He realized that ____. Therefore, he decided to ____ to ____. During ____, ____. Finally, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write seven connected sentences with one purpose to + verb, one instruction with told + person + to, one so that + could and four different time words.

formativeAssessment: Connects realisation, decision and purpose.
Keeps people and stages accurate.
Distinguishes purpose to + verb from instruction to + verb.
expectedResponses: Abraham realized that nobody was going to listen, so he decided to leave Babylon to spread Allah’s message in other lands; later, Allah commanded him to travel with Hagar and Ishmael to a lonely valley near Safa and Marwa.
content.transferTask: Explain a change of place in your own life or community using realized that, therefore, decided to, a purpose and a clear sequence.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the people and stages accurate and discover the two jobs of to + verb themselves?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, copy the three places into your notebook. Add a time word and one quoted action at each stage. One pair completes it on the board.
checkQuestions: How many places? (three)
What do you add at each stage? (a time word and a quoted action)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that Hagar and Ishmael appear only at the last stage. Listen in Activity 1 for learners who see that to + verb can be an instruction. Ask partners to circle the purpose and the time words.

exitTicket: Write one sentence where to + verb gives a purpose and one where it gives an instruction (told me to …).

rubricLevels.secure: Connects realisation, decision and purpose.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He realized …, so he decided to … to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the people and stages accurate.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three places on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells purpose to + verb from instruction to + verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Does this answer Why, or is it an order?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a cohesive journey paragraph.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the five-sentence frame.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham, Sarah and Lot travel to Syria and Palestine. The region's names differ in languages: Şam / Damascus, Filistin / Palestine, Mısır / Egypt.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do people from different countries help newcomers who arrive with a new belief or language? What helps a newcomer most in your town?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners avoid stereotypes about migrants. They describe one helpful action, such as explaining local rules politely.

content.chapter: 11. Hagar and Ishmael in the Valley
objectives: Show how Hagar’s trust (“Allah will never let us die …”) and her active effort (running between the hills) go together.
Trace need → search → the later practice of sa’y, keeping the story and the explanation of the practice separate.

Discover what the struggle phrases mean (ran out, needed to, started running, looking for, fearlessly) and use pray to + person + to + verb, the past continuous after “knew”, a plan to + verb and the language for explaining a practice (is known as, must, after + -ing, involves + -ing).
Connect responsibility with active care rather than passive waiting.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is about agency. Learners draw arrows from the need (food and water ran out) to every action Hagar takes, then draw a line under the story and write the later practice below it. Language discovery follows the same split: the story uses need to, started + -ing and looking for, while the explanatory paragraph uses is known as, must, after + -ing and involves + -ing. Abraham’s prayer is a Qur’anic prayer and Hagar’s words are a narrated saying: both are read calmly and intact and are never gapped; the Language Focus practises the narrator’s sentences instead.
priorKnowledge: must; start + -ing; to + verb for purpose; past continuous.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Trust is not presented as waiting: Hagar trusts Allah and also runs and searches.
The distances in the last sentence are background information, not the learning goal of the chapter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: meaning of the struggle phrases (ran out = there was none left · needed to · started running · looking for = trying to find · fearlessly: -less = without) · pray to + person + to + verb (prayed to Allah to protect them) · past continuous after a past verb (knew that Abraham was doing …) · a plan + to + verb (Allah’s plan to build the Holy House) · explaining a practice: is known as, must + base verb, after + -ing, involves + -ing.
Notice (Activity 1): after the matching, ask: “Which phrase shows the problem? Which shows what she had to do? Which show what she did?” Learners build the need → action chain from the phrases.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose to protect / was doing / to build, then complete the explanation of sa’y with is known as / must / after / involves and say why “knows as” and “must to” are wrong.
Likely errors: *prayed to Allah protecting them · *knew that Abraham is doing · *plan for build · *must to complete · *after perform the tawaf · *involves to walk.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences explaining a routine or practice they know (a school fire drill, a football warm-up, a family recipe), with need to, start + -ing, is known as, must, after + -ing and involves + -ing.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the prayer calmly in meaning groups: “O our LORD! | I have LEFT my FAMily | to STAY in a VALley with no FARMing, | near Your HOly HOUSE”.
Confidence stress: “alLAH will NEVer let us DIE; | he will SURELY proTECT us.”
Phrasal verb stress on the particle: “their FOOD and WAter ran OUT”.
Arabic terms said clearly inside English sentences: HAJJ, UM-rah, ta-WAF, sa’y (with a short catch in the middle).
Word focus: FEAR-less-ly, HELP-less-ly, RIT-u-al, ap-PROX-i-mate-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can you be confident about something and still need to work hard for it?” Collect one or two school examples (confident about a match, still train every day).
duringReading: Underline Hagar’s words of trust.
Mark the need (food and water ran out).
Number Hagar’s actions.
Draw a line before “This effort by Hagar is known as …” and label the part below it “the practice today”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the need → action chain in view.
Language Focus: Match the struggle phrases, choose the forms for purpose and background, then complete the explanation of the practice.
Write five sentences explaining a routine or practice you know.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Confident and still working hard, two school examples; 4–11 The teacher reads the prayer calmly as a model, then learners listen to the chapter and read along; 11–19 Need → action arrows in pairs: The need at the top, each of Hagar’s actions below with a quote, then a line and the practice today underneath, quick check that trust and effort appear together; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with the discovery questions, Activity 2 in pairs (the prayer is read intact, never gapped), Activity 3 individually with pair checking; 31–38 Use: Five sentences explaining a routine (A fire drill is known as … We must … After leaving the room, … It involves walking …), two learners read and the class names the rule and the order; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How do Hagar’s words and Hagar’s actions fit together?
What need starts her search?
How is the later practice connected to her effort?
interactiveTips: Use the Hagar’s Trust hotspot for her words and the Safa and Marwa hotspot for the search and the practice.
Replay “She helplessly started running from one hill to another looking for water and food.” and ask learners to count the actions.
Read the prayer and Hagar’s words intact; do not rewrite them in transfer tasks.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “The ____ ran out. She needed to ____. She started ____ing. She was looking for ____.” and for the practice “It is known as ____. People must ____ after ____ing.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences explaining a practice with is known as, must, after + -ing and involves + -ing, plus one sentence with “a plan to …”.

formativeAssessment: Shows Hagar as an active agent who also trusts.
Keeps the story and the explanation of the practice separate.
Uses must + base verb, after + -ing and involves + -ing correctly.
expectedResponses: Hagar trusted that Allah would protect them, and when the food and water ran out she ran between the two hills seven times looking for water; this effort is known as sa’y, which Muslims still complete after the tawaf.
content.transferTask: Explain a routine or practice from your life, including a need, the steps in order, one rule and what it involves.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect trust with action, and did they keep the story sequence and the explanatory paragraph distinct?

classroomManagement.instructions: Listen to my model reading of the prayer. Then, in pairs, draw the need at the top and Hagar’s actions below it with arrows and quotes. Add the practice today underneath.
checkQuestions: What goes at the top? (the need)
Do we gap or change the prayer? (no, we read it as it is)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that trust and effort appear together on the arrows. In Activity 2, make sure the prayer is read intact. In the Use task, ask the class to name the rule and the order.

exitTicket: Complete: “Our morning routine at school is known as ____. We must ____ after ____ing. It involves ____ing.”

rubricLevels.secure: Builds the chain from need to actions with quotes.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the need and two actions as a start.

rubricLevels.secure: Shows Hagar as active and trusting at the same time.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What did she believe? What did she do?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains a practice with is known as, must and involves + -ing.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the fire drill model.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the story and the explanation of the practice separate.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is this the story, or what Muslims do today?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Hagar runs between the hills, and the chapter connects this to the later practice of sa'y.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How would you explain sa'y to an English-speaking friend who has never heard of it? Which English words help (walk, between two hills, remember, effort)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Explaining a practice of your own culture clearly and calmly is an intercultural skill. Learners avoid untranslated terms without explanation.

content.chapter: 12. Zamzam and the City of Mecca
objectives: Distinguish the background actions (Ishmael crying, Hagar running) from the sudden event (the water starting to flow).
Separate the immediate relief from the longer development: The spring still exists, people came to settle, a city called Mecca was built.
Discover why the chapter uses was crying / was running but started flowing, and use when + past simple, still + present simple, because of + noun phrase and came to + verb.
Explain how one event can change a place over time.
content.pedagogy: Use two timelines: A short one for the immediate event and a long one for what changed over the years. Learners place chapter phrases on the right timeline and justify each choice. The key sentence is then discovered in context: You ask “Which actions were already happening, and which one is new?” and learners find that the past continuous sets the background and the past simple after “suddenly” interrupts it.
priorKnowledge: Past continuous and past simple; still; because / because of.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The water appears before people settle; settlement is a later result, not part of the same moment.
Learners may say “was seeing” or “is still existing”; see and exist are not normally used in the continuous.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: while + past continuous for background actions + suddenly + past simple for the new event · when + past simple for the moment that causes a reaction · no continuous with state and perception verbs (saw, exists) · still + present simple for a situation that continues until now · because of + noun phrase (vs because + clause) · came to + verb for purpose.
Notice (Activity 1): show the while-sentence. Ask: “Which actions were already happening? Which one is new? Which word warns us that something unexpected is coming?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct was seeing → saw and is still existing → still exists, then build the cause sentence and move “because of this sacred spring” to the front with a comma.
Likely errors: *When Hagar was seeing this · *is still existing · *because of this spring was sacred · *came for settle.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a real place that changed over time (their neighbourhood, a park, a new station), with while, suddenly or when, still, because of and came to; “Meanwhile” can link a second line of events.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Background with a level tune, then a pause and stress on the new event: “WHILE the LITtle CHILD ISHmael was CRYing with THIRST | and HAgar was RUNning between the two HILLS, | SUDdenly | WAter STARted FLOWing …”.
The /θ/ in thirst, and the cluster in “still exists” (/stɪl ɪɡˈzɪsts/).
-ed endings: started /ɪd/, shouted /ɪd/, collected /ɪd/, visited /ɪd/, gained /d/.
Word focus: his-TOR-ic, SA-cred, MEAN-while, ZAM-zam, MEC-ca, SET-tle.
beforeReading: Give a neutral example: “A new bridge opened in a small town.” Pairs say one thing that changed on the first day and one thing that changed over the next ten years.
duringReading: Mark the two background actions.
Circle “suddenly” and the new event.
Underline Hagar’s reaction with “When …”.
Build a long-term chain: fame → still exists → began to live → more people came → a city called Mecca.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the two timelines in view.
Language Focus: Discover background and sudden event in Activity 1, correct saw / still exists in Activity 2 and build the cause sentence in Activity 3.
Write five sentences about a place that changed over time.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: The new bridge, first day vs ten years later; 4–11 Listen and read, mark the background, “suddenly” and the reaction; 11–19 Two timelines in pairs: The moment (crying, running, water flowing, shout, drink, feed) and the long term (fame, still exists, people settle, Mecca, Abraham’s visits), each phrase quoted, then a gallery check where pairs compare with the next desk; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Which actions were already happening?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, with learners saying the cause sentence both ways; 31–38 Use: Five sentences about a place that changed (While people were …, suddenly … Because of …, more people came to … It still …), partners mark background, event and long-term change; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What was happening when the water appeared?
Which results were immediate, and which came over the years?
Why did more people come to the valley?
interactiveTips: Use the Zamzam Water hotspot for the immediate event and the “A Growing City” hotspot for the long-term change.
Replay the while-sentence and ask learners to clap once at “suddenly”.
Keep the two timelines on the board so the moment and the long-term development do not merge.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “While ____ was ____ing, suddenly ____. When ____ saw ____, ____. Because of ____, ____. It still ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences moving from a background to a sudden event and two later results, using while, suddenly, because of, came to and Meanwhile.

formativeAssessment: Separates background, sudden event and long-term change.
Uses the past simple for see and the present simple with still exists.
Uses because of with a noun phrase.
expectedResponses: While Ishmael was crying and Hagar was running, water suddenly started flowing; Hagar drank, collected it and fed her child, and later more people came to settle because of the spring and started building Mecca.
content.transferTask: Explain how one event changed a place you know, using background, a sudden event, cause and continuity language.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the immediate relief and the later settlement separate, and did they find the background / new-event rule from the sentence?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, draw two timelines: the moment and the long term. Put a quoted phrase on each. Then compare with the next desk.
checkQuestions: How many timelines? (two)
Who do you compare with? (the next desk)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that crying and running are background and water flowing is the sudden event. Listen for learners saying the cause sentence both ways. Ask partners to mark background, event and long-term change.

exitTicket: Write one while … suddenly … sentence about your day and one “still + present simple” sentence about your town.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates background, sudden event and long-term change.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Was it already happening?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses the past simple for saw and the present simple with still exists.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses because of with a noun phrase.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give “because of the spring” as a model.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains a long-term change in a place.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the five-sentence frame.

interculturalFocus.notice: Zamzam water helps Mecca grow into a city. Water and wells are at the centre of town life in many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Why do Ottoman cities have so many public fountains (çeşme), and who built them? Do English towns have public drinking fountains or village wells?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice that giving water to others is a shared kindness in many cultures.

objectives: Explain the command, Abraham’s request to Ishmael and Ishmael’s promise, and the work father and son do together.
Trace the Ka’ba from an ancient first sacred place that disappeared over time to its rebuilding and completion.

Discover how told / commanded + person + to report an instruction and will + verb gives a role or a promise, and use the sequence words (originally, over time, began to, After), for, Over the years and to + verb for purpose.
Synthesise the book: From Abraham’s search in Babylon to a message carried across generations, without adding details the book does not give.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 secures the story: Learners build a role chart (the command / Abraham / Ishmael / father and son together) and order the history of the building on sequence cards. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners sort the opening dialogue into instructions and promises and discover how “will” gives Ishmael a role and then becomes his promise; then they use the link words to write about something that continues after its founder. The message of tawhid at the end is read intact and never gapped.
priorKnowledge: tell + person + to; will for promises; after + past simple.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Abraham does not build alone; father and son find the foundations and build together.
The Ka’ba is not presented as a new invention; it was originally built as the first sacred place and disappeared over time.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: command / tell + person + to + verb for an instruction · will + verb for a role (you will help me) and a promise (I will help you for sure) · sequence of the building: Earlier state (was … originally built), change (but … over time), new start (began to construct), completion (After + past simple) · reference words (the old building, on it) · for + noun for who something is for · Over the centuries · to + verb for purpose.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort four parts into “what someone was told to do” / “what someone will do”. Ask: “Who tells whom? Who promises? Which words make the promise stronger?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Order the five parts about the building and name the word that helped each time, then complete the lines with for / Over the centuries / to and say why Since and so do not fit.
Likely errors: *told me do · *I will to help · *After he has built · *Since the years · *spread … for carry the message.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a project, tradition or idea that continues after its founder (a school club, a library, a family tradition), with told / asked + person + to, will, after, began to, to + verb and over the years.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast the instruction and the role: “alLAH TOLD me to DO an imPORtant TASK, | and YOU will HELP me in this TASK.”
The promise falls firmly: “I will HELP you for SURE↘.”
Pause after the time frame: “OVer the YEARS, | …”.
Arabic names inside English: KAA-ba (the Ka’ba), HAJJ.
Word focus: foun-DA-tions, con-STRUCT, AN-cient, o-RIG-i-nal-ly, pe-NIN-su-la, u-NIQUE.
beforeReading: Retrieve Chapters 11–12 in one minute: Pairs name the valley, the two hills, the spring and the city. Then ask: “What could father and son build together in this place?”
duringReading: Label the command and the instruction Abraham passes to Ishmael.
Mark Ishmael’s promise.
Number the history of the building: original → disappeared → foundations found → rebuilding → completion.
Underline who the Ka’ba was for and what Ishmael’s family carried.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and a bridge note with one instruction and one promise from the chapter.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on instruction and promise, the sequence of the building and purpose across generations.
Write five sentences about something that continues after its founder, then begin the whole-book review.
