metadata.title: Prophet Abraham — B1 Teacher Guide
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, inductive grammar from the story sentence and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 15 class periods: 11 chapters × 40 minutes; Chapters 8 and 13 × 40 + 40 minutes. The whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: Secondary-school learners studying English at approximately CEFR B1.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow a connected narrative, compare evidence, explain reasoning and produce short connected B1 speech and writing.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh), using the Language Focus attached to all thirteen story chapters, connected production about the learners’ own world and values shown as observable actions.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does (the rule is confirmed only afterwards), then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. Chapters 8 and 13 are divided into two 40-minute lessons rather than compressed. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 13 Quick Challenges, chapter-specific evidence checks, Language Focus tasks and production, connected oral and written transfer, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Language Review, Vocabulary Challenge and Final Challenge.

formative: Language Focus: Noticing and controlled practice
Connected B1 speaking and writing transfer

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs, with a short chapter-specific hook: An evidence question, a habit/event contrast, a mystery, a claim to test or a timeline prediction.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist, then read and follow the chapter’s own evidence structure: claim and evidence, habit and event, a reasoning chain, speaker and purpose, plan and final state, admission and refusal, danger and trust, route, need and action, background and sudden event, instruction and promise.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world. In the 40 + 40 chapters, Lesson 1 secures meaning and evidence and Lesson 2 develops language and production.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise the chapter Word Notes and the words needed for the chapter’s key relationship (claim/evidence, habit/event, need/action).
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, word parts (re-consider, fear-less-ly), image or audio before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the whole-book review sequence.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? Who is speaking? Had it happened yet?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: “could” in context (belief / real inability); named …, made from … ↔ relative clause; ago / when / From
Ch2: used to; while + past continuous; One day + past simple; not … but; bigger than; told … not to
Ch3: still + past continuous; Although; On the other hand; to for purpose; because; wondered if …; understood that …
Ch4: If … will … with two purposes; until; chose him to be; should + because; imperatives; stop + -ing
Ch5: got furious / did not give up / reconsider / ignored / though; because vs because of; when-clause; want + person + to
Ch6: was going to (future from the past); usually / so / until; began to … one after another; did not + verb; and then
Ch7: direct vs embedded questions; heard + person + -ing; what they heard; shocked to; because; so … that; If … then … meant
Ch8: passive without a doer; so … that; However; because; would for the future from the past; was used to + verb
Ch9: yet / however; order … to vs let / make + base verb; was unable to; only … has the power
Ch10: to + verb for purpose vs instruction; so that + could; decided to; During; Finally; was going to ↔ is going to
Ch11: ran out / needed to / started + -ing / looking for / -less; so that + may; let + base verb; will surely; is known as, must, after + -ing, involves + -ing
Ch12: while + past continuous + suddenly; when + past simple; no continuous with see / exist; still + present simple; because of; came to
Ch13: told / commanded + person + to; will for a role and a promise; originally, over time, began to, After; for; Over the years; to for purpose

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify and compare evidence, follow reasoning chains and discourse relationships, infer motivation and connect ideas across paragraphs.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: listen for gist, then replay targeted sentences to check evidence, signal words and pronunciation.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: make short claims, justify them with text evidence, respond to a partner and use chapter language in new, safe situations.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using the chapter patterns and revise them after peer feedback.

valuesFocus: D6 Honesty — distinguish claims from evidence and represent the source accurately
D10 Humility — stay open to evidence and admit a mistake rather than protect a weak claim
D12 Patience — keep trying with purpose under rejection or difficulty
D14 Respect — discuss belief, disagreement and family differences respectfully
D16 Responsibility — connect guidance, family care, mission and assigned tasks with responsible action
D20 Helpfulness — recognize cooperation and care as observable actions
languageFocus: Every one of the 13 story chapters has an active Language Focus set built as notice → build → use.
Use Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form does before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At B1 the last step is always connected production about the learners’ own world, not a retelling of the chapter.
For 40 + 40 chapters, use the second lesson for Language Focus and connected production rather than re-reading the whole story.
After Chapter 13, use the real review order: Knowledge Check → Language Review → Vocabulary Challenge → Master Glossary → Final Challenge.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: One evidence sentence at a time, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal before writing. Extend by combining more chapter patterns or adding a second evidence relationship, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful discussion
notes: Keep religious and historical claims inside the wording of this B1 story; do not add legends, dates or details the book does not give.

Qur’anic references, the prayers of Abraham (pbuh), Hagar’s words of trust and the message of tawhid are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped by the teacher, “corrected” or rewritten. Where a Language Focus item uses a line from a prayer, read the whole line intact after the answer.
Discuss the idols and the people’s beliefs through evidence and respectful language; never turn evidence work into mocking people, communities or objects that others hold sacred.
Prophets, angels and the scenes of threat, punishment, fire and the killing in Chapter 9 are never role-played or acted out; the teacher reads these sentences once, calmly and factually.
In Chapter 8, stay within what the source states: Abraham trusted Allah and knew Allah would never leave him alone; the chapter does not say he knew how he would be saved.
Do not present learners’ reflections or value-transfer examples as new religious facts.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh) connects a journey from Babylon to the valley of Mecca with questions every community faces: How we test ideas with evidence, how we disagree respectfully, how water makes a place liveable and how a place can welcome all people.

themes.title: Thinking with evidence:
themes.description: Abraham tests each possibility and changes his view when the evidence changes (Chapter 3). Discuss how checking evidence protects us from false news and rumours today.

themes.title: Respectful disagreement:
themes.description: Abraham speaks to his father with “O my father” even when they disagree (Chapter 4). Discuss how people with different views can talk without insults at home, at school and online.

themes.title: Water and community:
themes.description: Because of the Zamzam spring, more people came to settle in the valley (Chapter 12). Connect this with the value of clean water for communities around the world and in your own town.

themes.title: A place for all people:
themes.description: The Ka’ba was built as a place of worship for all people of different races and colors (Chapter 13). Discuss how schools and cities can welcome people of every background.

actions: Check one news story or message you received this week with a second source before you share it.
Make a class water-saving plan with three realistic actions for school and home.
Write three class rules for respectful disagreement, including online messages.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter is …

miniProject.title: Water Makes a Place
miniProject.desc: In groups, find out where your town or school gets its water and how the place grew around it. Make a one-page poster or a short audio clip in clear English: Start with one sentence from Chapter 12, then explain your own town with background and event (while … suddenly …), cause (because of …), continuity (still …) and change over time (Over the years, …). Finish with one realistic water-saving action.

reflectivePrompt.title: Changing My Mind
reflectivePrompt.desc: Abraham changed his view each time the evidence changed, while the people in Chapter 7 knew Abraham was right but were too arrogant to admit they were wrong. Write six to eight sentences about a time when you changed your mind after new evidence, or found it hard to admit a mistake. What happened, and what did you learn?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use a value only where chapter events genuinely support it. Require source evidence before moving to a realistic, age-appropriate action. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty appears through accurate evidence use and willingness to say when a claim is not supported.

items.label: D10 Humility
items.value: Humility appears through openness to correction rather than arrogance in the face of evidence.

items.label: D12 Patience
items.value: Patience is connected with continued, purposeful effort under rejection or difficulty.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect shapes how disagreement, belief and family differences are discussed.

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility appears through guidance, family care, mission, cooperation and assigned tasks.

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness appears through concrete cooperation and care.

What realistic action could show the same value?
Which part is source evidence and which part is your own application?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Follow the sequence: The sun sets → Abraham’s conclusion → prayer for help → responsibility → the conversation with his father.
lookFor: Instruction: In pairs, make a speaker map: for each spoken line, write the speaker, the words and the purpose. Purposes are question, prayer for help, instruction or threat.
Check questions: What three things do you write for each line? (speaker, words, purpose) / How many purposes can you choose from? (four)

While learners work: Check that the father’s if-sentence is labelled a threat. In Activity 1, listen for who speaks and what he wants. In the school scene, ask partners to label the purpose of each sentence.
Evidence of “Sequence”: Orders the sunset, the conclusion and the prayer.

peerObservation.focus: Explain that the people’s embarrassment did not change their anger and arrogance.
lookFor: Instruction: In pairs, complete the claim chart: claim, example, challenge, result. Then vote with the class: does the example prove the claim? Give a reason.
Check questions: How many columns? (four) / What do we vote on? (if the example proves the claim)

While learners work: Listen for reasons in the vote, not just yes or no. During the board contrast, check “ordered … to bring” and “let … live” without to. In the Use task, check for However before the result.
Evidence of “Claim precision”: States Nimrod’s claim precisely.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the B1 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the B1 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

actionResearch.question: Can learners separate a past habit (used to) from a single event (One day + past simple) in their own writing, as Chapter 2 does?

objectives: I can explain what the people of Babylon worshipped and why Abraham questioned it.

content.grammarFocus: Decide what could shows in “a god which could help or harm him”, expand short describing phrases into full clauses (a boy who was named Abraham, statues which were made from wood and stone), then place the story in time with ago, when and From.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: Abraham and His Father’s Idols

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find what happened to the star and to the moon, and read the words after because. Choose the answer that is true for both of them, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone examining two possible explanations for an everyday situation. Use Although or On the other hand, test a possibility with a question, and end with a conclusion (I understood that …) and a reason.

whatToNotice: Abraham tests each possibility in the same way: He asks a question, watches what happens and reaches a conclusion.
Notice “they were still showing love and respect to idols.” Still shows that years passed, but the people did not change.
readListen: Look at The Star and the Moon hotspot. What happens to a star and to the moon every night?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 2 again and mark each question and each conclusion.
Open the picture hotspots “The Cave” and “The Star and the Moon” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Abraham knew about Allah and why he felt sad.
Paragraph 2: find where Abraham went and what he did there.
Paragraph 2: find his reason for rejecting the star, and what he understood when the moon faded.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: Creator, countryside, cave, faded.
“But when the moon faded, he understood that it could not be his Lord.” Did the moon disappear suddenly or slowly?
Write one sentence with countryside and one with faded.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Abraham decided that the star and the moon could not be his Lord. Read the end of paragraph 2 and look for because.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Find what happened to the star and to the moon, and read the words after because.
Choose the answer that is true for both of them, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the test Abraham used for the star and the moon?
Can I report his question with if or whether?
Can I say what still shows about the people?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone examining two possible explanations for an everyday situation. Use Although or On the other hand, test a possibility with a question, and end with a conclusion (I understood that …) and a reason.
content.reflectionPrompt: Abraham did not accept an answer until he had tested it. When is it wise to ask “Could this be …?” before you believe something?

objectives: I can explain what the setting sun taught Abraham.
I can compare Abraham’s prayer with his father’s threat.
I can use If + present, will …, should + verb and stop + -ing.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Compare the purpose of the two if-sentences, choose until and to be (chose him to be His Messenger), then fix should guide and Stop worshipping.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: SUN-rise, cre-A-tions, PROS-trat-ed, MES-sen-ger. Say the father’s threat with a strong, falling voice and Abraham’s prayer softly.
content.lessonPlan: Look at The Setting Sun hotspot. Why is the sun a stronger test than the star and the moon? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraphs 2 and 4 again and compare the two if-sentences.
discussionPoints: Abraham said, “O my father, follow me”, and his father threatened him. How can you disagree with someone you love and still speak with respect?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Setting Sun” and “The Right Way”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again and stop at the end of each paragraph. Remember: the sky comes before the prayer, and the prayer comes before Abraham goes home. Put the events in order again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a person who realises a responsibility. Use when, should … because …, one direct instruction, and an If …, I will … response.

whatToNotice: Two if-sentences have the same form but a different purpose: one is a prayer for guidance, the other is a threat.
Notice “Allah could not be one of the creations. Allah is the Creator of everything.” The second sentence gives the reason for the first.
readListen: Look at The Setting Sun hotspot. Why is the sun a stronger test than the star and the moon?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraphs 2 and 4 again and compare the two if-sentences.
Open the picture hotspots “The Setting Sun” and “The Right Way” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find how long Abraham stayed and why he thought the sun could be his Lord.
Paragraph 2: find what he understood when the sun set, and what he did next.
Paragraphs 3–4: find why Abraham should guide his people, what he asked his father, and how his father answered.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: sunrise, creations, prostrated, stone.
“If you do not stop speaking like this, I will stone you.” Is stone a noun or a verb here?
Write one sentence with sunrise and one with creations.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put five events in order, from the sun to Azer’s anger. Follow the chapter paragraph by paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter again and stop at the end of each paragraph.
Remember: the sky comes before the prayer, and the prayer comes before Abraham goes home.
Put the events in order again.
selfCheck: Can I explain what the setting sun proved to Abraham?
Can I explain the different purposes of the two if-sentences?
Can I say should guide and stop worshipping correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a person who realises a responsibility. Use when, should … because …, one direct instruction, and an If …, I will … response.
content.reflectionPrompt: Abraham said, “O my father, follow me”, and his father threatened him. How can you disagree with someone you love and still speak with respect?

objectives: I can explain Abraham’s reasons and the people’s one reason.
I can explain why following our fathers is not proof.
I can use because, because of this, when and want + person + to.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Match phrases such as got furious, did not give up and ignored with their meanings, choose because, because of this and when, then rewrite “He wanted them to reconsider their beliefs.” as Abraham’s own words (I want you to reconsider …) and move the when-clause to the front.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: re-con-SID-er, FU-ri-ous, ig-NORED. Say “O people!” as a strong call, and stop briefly at the semicolon in “We saw our fathers worship them; because of this, we do the same.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Following Their Fathers hotspot. Is doing what our parents did a good reason for a belief? Listen once and follow the text. Read the chapter again and mark Abraham’s reasons in one color and the people’s reason in another.
discussionPoints: Abraham did not give up, even when people got furious and ignored him. When is it worth trying again, and when should you give someone time to think?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Public Call” and “Following Their Fathers”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find the people’s answer: “We saw our fathers worship them”. Then read what Abraham says the statues have no power to do. Ask: Is a habit the same as evidence? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone trying to change another person’s mind. Give a reason with because, show an attempt, show that the person did not give up, and end with a contrasting response using though or but.

whatToNotice: The chapter is one long paragraph: A call, an angry reaction, a question, the people’s answer, Abraham’s evidence and a final response.
Notice “They ignored him, though.” Though at the end shows a result different from what Abraham wanted.
readListen: Look at the Following Their Fathers hotspot. Is doing what our parents did a good reason for a belief?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read the chapter again and mark Abraham’s reasons in one color and the people’s reason in another.
Open the picture hotspots “Public Call” and “Following Their Fathers” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Beginning: Find what Abraham told the people and why he did not worship their idols.
Middle: Find the people’s only reason and the words that introduce their result.
End: Find what Allah gives Abraham, what the statues cannot do, and how the people responded.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: give up, harm, heals, reconsider.
“He wanted them to reconsider their beliefs.” What does re- add to consider?
Write one sentence with did not give up and one with heals.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the people’s reason was weak. Compare their answer in the middle of the paragraph with Abraham’s words about what Allah gives him.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find the people’s answer: “We saw our fathers worship them”.
Then read what Abraham says the statues have no power to do.
Ask: Is a habit the same as evidence? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the difference between a habit and evidence?
Can I use because and because of this correctly?
Can I say what I want another person to do with want + person + to?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone trying to change another person’s mind. Give a reason with because, show an attempt, show that the person did not give up, and end with a contrasting response using though or but.
content.reflectionPrompt: Abraham did not give up, even when people got furious and ignored him. When is it worth trying again, and when should you give someone time to think?

objectives: I can explain Abraham’s plan and why he waited for the celebration.
I can explain why he did not break the largest statue.
I can use was going to, so, until and leave + object + describing word.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what “what he was going to do” means, complete the lines with usually, so and until, then rebuild “He hung the axe around its neck and then hurried back home” and see which action came first.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: cel-e-BRA-tion, ri-DIC-u-lous, FOOL-ish-ness. Read Abraham’s joke lightly: “Why don’t you eat the food? It is getting cold.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Food for the Idols hotspot. Why is food in front of a statue strange? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 1 again and number the steps of the plan.
discussionPoints: Abraham used a joke to show that the statues could not even eat. Can humour help people see a mistake? When can it hurt?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Empty Town” and “Food for the Idols”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Read what Abraham did with the largest statue. Compare the sentence with the text word by word, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a person carrying out a careful plan in a new situation. Show the intention, the chance, the timing with until, and the end with did not + verb and and then.

whatToNotice: Every step is deliberate: a decision, a plan, a chance (the empty town), the action and a final state.
Notice “what he was going to do”: when he made the plan, breaking the idols was still in the future.
readListen: Look at the Food for the Idols hotspot. Why is food in front of a statue strange?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 1 again and number the steps of the plan.
Open the picture hotspots “Empty Town” and “Food for the Idols” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Abraham decided, why the town was empty and what he took with him.
Paragraph 1: find his joke to the statues and the writer’s comment on offering them food.
Paragraph 2: find how he broke the idols and the three things he did at the end.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: foolishness, celebration, axe, ridiculous.
“Offering food to these statues was so ridiculous.” Whose opinion is this: Abraham’s, the people’s or the writer’s?
Write one sentence with celebration and one with ridiculous.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will decide if a sentence about the statues is true or false. Read paragraph 2 carefully before you answer.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Read what Abraham did with the largest statue.
Compare the sentence with the text word by word, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I tell the plan in four or five steps?
Can I explain why Abraham chose the day of the celebration?
Can I use did not + verb and and then in my own sentences?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a person carrying out a careful plan in a new situation. Show the intention, the chance, the timing with until, and the end with did not + verb and and then.
content.reflectionPrompt: Abraham used a joke to show that the statues could not even eat. Can humour help people see a mistake? When can it hurt?

objectives: I can explain how Abraham used the people’s own words against their belief.
I can explain why the people refused the truth they felt.
I can use because, so … that and if … then to explain a reason, a result and a consequence.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort direct questions from question ideas inside a longer sentence (find out who did this, ask that statue if it can speak), fix speaking, what they heard and shocked to see, then choose because, that and meant to explain the reason, the result and the consequence.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: AR-ro-gant, dis-PLEASED, FORE-fa-thers. Smashed has one syllable. Say “Burn him! Burn him!” with strong stress and a falling voice.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Public Questioning hotspot. Why question someone in front of everyone? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 3 again and mark the reason for their shame and the reason they still refused.
discussionPoints: The people knew Abraham was right, but pride stopped them from admitting it. Why is it hard to admit we were wrong, and how can we make it easier for others?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Smashed Statues” and “Public Questioning”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Read the sentence with because, then the sentence that starts with But. Ask what they would lose if they accepted the truth, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a disagreement in a new situation. Report what someone heard, include a question idea (find out who …), and explain a reason and an if … then consequence.

whatToNotice: The key moment is “You are well aware that these idols don’t speak!” The people themselves give Abraham his proof.
Notice the two feelings in paragraph 3: shame, then pride. But shows which one won.
readListen: Look at the Public Questioning hotspot. Why question someone in front of everyone?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 3 again and mark the reason for their shame and the reason they still refused.
Open the picture hotspots “Smashed Statues” and “Public Questioning” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find how the people found out who broke the idols and what Abraham answered.
Paragraph 2: find the people’s words and Abraham’s three questions.
Paragraph 3: find why they felt shame, why they could not admit it, and what it would mean about their forefathers.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: smashed, displeased, shame, arrogant.
“But they were so arrogant that they couldn’t accept the truth”: What was the result of their arrogance?
Write one sentence with shame and one with displeased.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the people shouted even though they felt Abraham was right. Read paragraph 3 and look for the word But.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Read the sentence with because, then the sentence that starts with But.
Ask what they would lose if they accepted the truth, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain how Abraham used the people’s words as evidence?
Can I explain the fight between shame and pride?
Can I use so … that for a strong quality and its result?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a disagreement in a new situation. Report what someone heard, include a question idea (find out who …), and explain a reason and an if … then consequence.
content.reflectionPrompt: The people knew Abraham was right, but pride stopped them from admitting it. Why is it hard to admit we were wrong, and how can we make it easier for others?

objectives: I can describe how big and dangerous the fire was.
I can explain why Abraham stayed calm.
I can explain why the chapter uses the passive and would.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort passive sentences (was collected, were tied, was thrown) from active ones, complete so … that, However and because, then choose happened, would and to so that the story looks forward from the past.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: CAT-a-pult, FIRE-wood, ap-PROACH. Stress so in “The fire was so big that people couldn’t approach it.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the A Huge Fire hotspot. What details show how big a fire is? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraphs 2 and 3 again and underline the two so … that sentences.
discussionPoints: Abraham said, “Nothing from you!” even in the flames because he trusted Allah. What helps you stay calm when something frightening happens?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Huge Fire” and “Cool and Safe”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Read the sentence with because and the sentence after it. Check when Gabriel came: Before the fire or in the flames? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation with pressure and an unexpected result. Use so … that, however or because, knew/thought that … would, and turned out to be.

whatToNotice: The chapter builds danger step by step (firewood, heat, a catapult) and then turns it around: The fire becomes cool and safe.
Notice “Firewood was collected” and “was thrown”: the chapter does not say who did these actions because the focus is on what happened.
readListen: Look at the A Huge Fire hotspot. What details show how big a fire is?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraphs 2 and 3 again and underline the two so … that sentences.
Open the picture hotspots “A Huge Fire” and “Cool and Safe” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 2: find how big the fire was, how Abraham felt and why.
Paragraphs 3–4: find why people came from many towns and what a catapult was used for.
Paragraphs 5–6: find Abraham’s answer to Angel Gabriel, what Allah commanded and what the fire burnt.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: firewood, approach, flames, catapult.
“The heat was so strong that even birds couldn’t fly over the rising flames.” What does even add?
Write one sentence with approach and one with flames.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Abraham stayed calm. Read paragraph 2 and find the sentence with because.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Read the sentence with because and the sentence after it.
Check when Gabriel came: Before the fire or in the flames? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I describe the fire with two so … that sentences?
Can I explain where Abraham’s calm came from?
Can I explain why the chapter does not say who threw him?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation with pressure and an unexpected result. Use so … that, however or because, knew/thought that … would, and turned out to be.
content.reflectionPrompt: Abraham said, “Nothing from you!” even in the flames because he trusted Allah. What helps you stay calm when something frightening happens?

objectives: I can explain why the miracle did not change the people.
I can explain Nimrod’s claim and why Abraham’s challenge showed it was false.
I can use yet and however, and the right verb form after order, let and make.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what yet shows in the first sentence, fix ordered his guards to bring, let the second slave live and make the sun rise, then say “was unable to do this” in two other ways (could not do, was not able to do).
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: MIR-a-cle, OR-di-nar-y, NIM-rod. Say Abraham’s challenge as a real question with a rising voice: “Can you make the sun rise from the west?”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Nimrod’s Claim hotspot. What did Nimrod say he could do? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraphs 4–6 again and write who says each sentence.
discussionPoints: Abraham did not argue with anger; he asked one clear question that Nimrod could not answer. How can a good question be stronger than a loud argument?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Nimrod’s Claim” and “The Sun from the West”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraphs 4–6. Check who says “I can …” and who asks about the sun. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation in which someone makes a claim and another person tests it. Include a claim with can, a decision with so, a challenge, and a result such as was unable to.

whatToNotice: A miracle usually changes people, but here it does not: “yet their anger and arrogance remained unchanged.”
Notice the steps of the debate: A claim (“I can give life and death”), an example with two slaves, then a test only Allah can pass.
readListen: Look at the Nimrod’s Claim hotspot. What did Nimrod say he could do?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraphs 4–6 again and write who says each sentence.
Open the picture hotspots “Nimrod’s Claim” and “The Sun from the West” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraphs 1–2: find how the people felt after the miracle and what did not change.
Paragraph 3: find what Nimrod realized and what he decided.
Paragraphs 4–6: find Abraham’s answer, Nimrod’s example and Abraham’s challenge.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: miracle, rage, guards, ordinary.
“He realized that Abraham was not an ordinary person”: What made Nimrod think this?
Write one sentence with rage and one with ordinary.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four steps of the debate with what was said or done. Read paragraphs 4–6 and note who speaks each time.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraphs 4–6.
Check who says “I can …” and who asks about the sun.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why Nimrod’s example did not prove his claim?
Can I explain why the sun challenge ended the debate?
Can I use let and make without to?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation in which someone makes a claim and another person tests it. Include a claim with can, a decision with so, a challenge, and a result such as was unable to.
content.reflectionPrompt: Abraham did not argue with anger; he asked one clear question that Nimrod could not answer. How can a good question be stronger than a loud argument?

objectives: I can explain why Abraham left Babylon and what he hoped to do.
I can follow the stages of his long journey.
I can separate to + verb for a purpose from to + verb for an instruction.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort to + verb for a purpose (to spread Allah’s message) from to + verb after command or tell (told his wife to stay), choose to leave, During and Finally, then turn “nobody was going to listen” into Abraham’s own thought.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: CAM-el-back, TI-ring, PAL-es-tine. Pause at the comma after Therefore: “Therefore, he decided to leave Babylon …”.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Toward New Lands hotspot. Why do people leave their homeland? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 2 again and circle Therefore, During and soon.
discussionPoints: Abraham left his homeland not to give up, but to take the message further. When can leaving a place be a way of continuing, not stopping?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Toward New Lands” and “Lonely Valley”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Read the sentence before Therefore and the sentence after it. Ask: Did someone tell him to leave, or did he decide? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say five connected sentences about a new journey or change of place. Connect a realization, a decision with therefore or so, a purpose, events during the journey and an end point with finally.

whatToNotice: The chapter is a chain: Few believers → a realization → Therefore, a decision → a long journey → a lonely valley.
Notice “so that his child could teach people about Allah”: even his prayer for a child had a purpose.
readListen: Look at the Toward New Lands hotspot. Why do people leave their homeland?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 2 again and circle Therefore, During and soon.
Open the picture hotspots “Toward New Lands” and “Lonely Valley” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the two people who shared Abraham’s faith.
Paragraph 2: find what Abraham realized, where he traveled, and why he asked Allah for a child.
Paragraph 3: find what Allah commanded, where they arrived and what Abraham told his wife.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: faith, spread, camelback, tiring.
“It was a long, hot, and tiring journey.” Which of the three adjectives is a Word Note, and what does it tell you?
Write one sentence with spread and one with faith.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Abraham decided to leave Babylon. Read the beginning of paragraph 2 and find Therefore.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Read the sentence before Therefore and the sentence after it.
Ask: Did someone tell him to leave, or did he decide? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the reason for the journey and its purpose?
Can I retell the journey with During, soon and Finally?
Can I show two different jobs of to + verb?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say five connected sentences about a new journey or change of place. Connect a realization, a decision with therefore or so, a purpose, events during the journey and an end point with finally.
content.reflectionPrompt: Abraham left his homeland not to give up, but to take the message further. When can leaving a place be a way of continuing, not stopping?

content.chapter: Chapter 11: Hagar and Ishmael in the Valley
objectives: I can explain how Hagar showed both trust and effort.
I can explain the link between Hagar’s running and the ritual of sa’y.
I can explain a practice with is known as, must, after + -ing and involves.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Match phrases such as ran out, needed to and looking for with their meanings, choose to protect, was doing and to build, then complete the explanation of sa’y with is known as, must, after and involves.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: FEAR-less-ly, RIT-u-al, ap-PROX-i-mate-ly. Say the numbers: one hundred and thirty meters, three hundred meters. Read Hagar’s words with a firm, calm voice.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Hagar’s Trust hotspot. How can a person show trust in a hard situation? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 3 again and separate the story part from the explanation of the ritual.
discussionPoints: Hagar trusted Allah and still ran seven times between the hills. What does it mean to trust and also do your best?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Hagar’s Trust” and “Safa and Marwa”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Find what Hagar did when the food and water ran out. Ask: Did she only wait? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say five connected sentences about a routine, practice or difficult situation outside the story. Include a need, the start of an action, a rule with must, an order with after + -ing, and what the practice involves.

whatToNotice: Hagar trusted Allah, but she did not only wait: When the food and water ran out, she ran between the hills.
Notice the change of time in paragraph 3: the story is in the past, but “Even today, Muslims must complete the ritual” is in the present because it is still a rule.
readListen: Look at the Hagar’s Trust hotspot. How can a person show trust in a hard situation?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 3 again and separate the story part from the explanation of the ritual.
Open the picture hotspots “Hagar’s Trust” and “Safa and Marwa” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Abraham asked Allah for and what Hagar knew.
Paragraph 2: find what Hagar said when Abraham left them.
Paragraph 3: find what the valley did not have, what Hagar did when the food ran out, and how far Safa and Marwa are from the Ka’ba.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: fearlessly, ran out, ritual, approximately.
“But soon their food and water ran out.” Was there any food left?
Write one sentence with approximately and one with fearlessly.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will decide if a sentence about Hagar is true or false. Read her words in paragraph 2 and what she did in paragraph 3.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Find what Hagar did when the food and water ran out.
Ask: Did she only wait? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain how Hagar joined trust with effort?
Can I explain what sa’y is and why Muslims do it?
Can I use must and after + -ing to explain a practice?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say five connected sentences about a routine, practice or difficult situation outside the story. Include a need, the start of an action, a rule with must, an order with after + -ing, and what the practice involves.
content.reflectionPrompt: Hagar trusted Allah and still ran seven times between the hills. What does it mean to trust and also do your best?

content.chapter: Chapter 12: Zamzam and the City of Mecca
objectives: I can explain how the water appeared and what Hagar did.
I can explain how one spring led to a new city.
I can use while + past continuous for the background and the past simple for a sudden event.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Explain why the writer uses was crying and was running but started flowing, fix saw and still exists, then build “More people came to settle there because of this sacred spring” with the cause at the end or at the start.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: ZAM-zam, his-TOR-ic, FLOW-ing. Read the background slowly, “While the little child Ishmael was crying with thirst”, then say suddenly with more force.

metadata.title: Abraham B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh) on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the 13 chapters of the story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh).
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
Connect trust, honesty and effort with real actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the main idea, once to follow the exact words.
points: First listening: What is the chapter about?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence and say it with the same pauses.

sections.title: 3. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has four Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 4. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 5. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has four Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): choose, sort, rewrite or correct forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say four or five connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work one paragraph at a time.
Use the hotspots to get the big picture first.
Write a one-line summary of each paragraph.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: Abraham’s story links belief with evidence, honesty, trust and effort. Connect each value to one action.
points: Think with evidence: Test an idea instead of only following habit (Chapters 3, 5).
Respect in disagreement: Speak kindly to family even when you disagree (Chapters 4, 5).
Honesty: Admit a mistake even when pride says no (Chapter 7).
Trust and effort: Trust Allah and still do your best (Chapters 8, 11).
A place for everyone: People of all races and colors are welcome (Chapter 13).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
